q: Electrical energy can be transformed into a wide variety of other useful forms of energy.
e: True. Electrical energy is what a current carries through a circuit, later turned into heat, light or motion. Be transformed into a wide variety of other useful forms of energy.

q: The transformation of electrical energy into heat energy is very useful and important.
e: True. Electrical energy is what a current carries through a circuit, later turned into heat, light or motion. The transformation of electrical energy into heat energy is very useful and important.

q: Electrical energy is provided by sources of electromotive force such as resistors and capacitors.
e: False. The right claim is this: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into electrical form. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. The printed line wrongly says electrical energy is provided by sources of electromotive force such as resistors and capacitors.

q: A steady current will flow through the conductor if a steady potential difference is maintained between its ends by using batteries and generators.
e: True. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. Potential difference is maintained between its ends by using batteries and generators.

q: Batteries and generators are called sources of electromotive force.
e: True. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. Batteries and generators are called sources of electromotive force.

q: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from electrical form into other forms.
e: False. The right claim is this: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into electrical form. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. The printed line wrongly says the sources of electromotive force convert energy from electrical form into other forms.

q: A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy to provide electrical power.
e: True. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy to provide electrical power.

q: In an electric generator, heat energy is converted into electrical energy.
e: False. The right claim is this: In an electric generator, mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy. Electrical energy is what a current carries through a circuit, later turned into heat, light or motion. The printed line wrongly says in an electric generator, heat energy is converted into electrical energy.

q: A source of electromotive force has a positive terminal and a negative terminal.
e: True. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. A source of electromotive force has a positive terminal and a negative terminal.

q: The positive charges are sent from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.
e: False. The right claim is this: The positive charges are sent from the negative terminal to the positive terminal within the source. The printed line wrongly says the positive charges are sent from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.

q: The main function of the source is to send negative charges from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.
e: True. This main function of the source is to send negative charges from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source. Charges from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.

q: Electromotive force, abbreviated as emf, is the amount of energy provided by the battery per unit charge to move round the complete circuit.
e: True. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. By the battery per unit charge to move round the complete circuit.

q: Electromotive force is measured in unit of ampere ($A$).
e: False. The right claim is this: The unit of electromotive force is volt, equivalent to joule per coulomb of electric charge. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. The printed line wrongly says electromotive force is measured in unit of ampere (A).

q: One volt is equivalent to joule per coulomb of electric charge ($J C^{-1}$).
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. One volt is equivalent to joule per coulomb of electric charge (J C^-1).

q: Despite its name, electromotive force is actually a physical force.
e: False. The right claim is this: Despite its name, electromotive force is not actually a force. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. The printed line wrongly says despite its name, electromotive force is actually a physical force.

q: Generally, a source of electromotive force has an internal resistance.
e: True. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises. Generally, a source of electromotive force has an internal resistance.

q: The internal resistance of a battery depends on its size, chemical properties, life time, and temperature.
e: True. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises. A battery depends on its size, chemical properties, life time, and temperature.

q: A battery which has an internal resistance $r$ must be viewed as a resistor of resistance $r$ connected in parallel to the battery.
e: False. The right claim is this: A battery which has an internal resistance r must be viewed as having a resistor of resistance r connected in series to the battery. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises. The printed line wrongly says a battery which has an internal resistance r must be viewed as a resistor of resistance r connected in parallel to the battery.

q: By Ohm's law, the potential difference across the external resistor is $V = IR$.
e: True. Resistance opposes current and turns electrical energy into heat. The relation in this line is V = IR.

q: The work done in moving a unit positive charge from one end to another of the internal resistance $r$ of the battery is $Ir$.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. To another of the internal resistance r of the battery is Ir.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is $IR - Ir$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is IR+Ir, which is the emf E of the battery. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. The printed line wrongly says the total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is IR - Ir.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is the emf $E$ of the battery.
e: True. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. Charge round the complete circuit is the emf E of the battery.

q: The circuit equation is $E = I(R - r)$.
e: False. The right claim is this: The equation E=IR+Ir is called the circuit equation. The printed line wrongly says the circuit equation is E = I(R - r).

q: The potential difference between the terminals of a battery when it is connected to an external circuit is given by $V = E - Ir$.
e: True. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. The relation in this line is V = E - Ir.

q: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always greater than its emf.
e: False. The right claim is this: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always less than its emf. Emf is energy per coulomb that a source pumps around a complete loop. The printed line wrongly says when a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always greater than its emf.

q: The potential difference across the terminals of a battery connected to an external circuit is called the terminal voltage (or available voltage) of the battery.
e: True. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. Circuit is called the terminal voltage (or available voltage) of the battery.

q: Electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.
e: False. The right claim is this: Electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery in an open circuit. Potential difference is the electrical push between two points; no push, no current. The printed line wrongly says electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.

q: Terminal voltage is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.
e: True. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises. The two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.

q: Thus, emf is a closed-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is an open-circuit voltage.
e: False. The right claim is this: Thus, emf is an open-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is a closed-circuit voltage. Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points. The printed line wrongly says thus, emf is a closed-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is an open-circuit voltage.

q: Charging a battery means the chemical energy of the battery which has been used up is now supplied back by electrical energy from some external source.
e: True. While charging, plate voltage climbs toward the battery value as 1 minus a decaying exponential. Up is now supplied back by electrical energy from some external source.

q: In charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to $E - Ir$.
e: False. The right claim is this: When charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to E + Ir. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and holds a pd at its terminals. The printed line wrongly says in charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to E - Ir.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when open circuit (not in use) is $V = E$.
e: True. Terminal voltage is emf minus Ir, so it sags when the load current rises. The relation in this line is V = E.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when charging is $V > E$.
e: True. Voltage is potential difference, energy per unit charge between two points. The terminal voltage of a battery when charging is V > E.
